name: Message queues
summary: A to-do list between services: each job is done once, by one worker.
howItWorks: Producers drop messages into the queue and move on. Workers pull a message, process it and delete it when done. If a worker crashes mid-job, the message reappears after a visibility timeout and another worker retries it. The queue absorbs bursts so a slow system downstream isn’t overwhelmed, and you go faster by adding workers.
analogy: The ticket rail in a restaurant kitchen. Waiters clip orders up, cooks take the next one, and each order is cooked exactly once.
useWhen: Background jobs: emails, reports, image processing
Smoothing bursts so a database or API sees a steady rate
Retrying flaky work, with a dead-letter queue for messages that keep failing
avoidWhen: Several systems each need every message; use pub/sub or a stream
You may want to replay old messages; once deleted they’re gone
example: A checkout service enqueues “send receipt” jobs. During a flash sale 5,000 arrive in one minute. Two workers drain them over the next few minutes, and the email provider never sees more than its rate limit.

diagram.caption: Checkout bursts faster than two workers can keep up, so jobs pile up in the queue. Each worker takes the next job only when it’s free, and every job is handled once.

story: Message queues are almost as old as networked computing. IBM announced its Queued Telecommunications Access Method (QTAM) for System/360 mainframes in 1965, and banks and airlines pushed the idea further, because a lost, corrupted or duplicated transaction meant lost money or a lost seat. The point, as IBM’s Andy Stanford-Clark puts it, was to let systems work without being in “strict synchronous lockstep”: the sender drops a message and carries on, and the receiver picks it up when it’s ready.

IBM’s MQSeries, introduced in 1993, made the queue a product that connected applications across different machines, and, according to IBM, is still used by 98 of the top 100 global banks. Microsoft followed with MSMQ in 1997, and Java’s JMS API (1998) let Java programs use existing products such as MQSeries. Those products were proprietary and didn’t talk to each other, so in 2003 John O’Hara at JPMorgan began designing the open AMQP protocol, which RabbitMQ implemented as open source in 2007.

Cloud providers then turned the queue into a utility. Amazon SQS, in beta from 2004 and generally available in 2006, had no broker to run and charged per request; Google, Microsoft and others followed. The idea keeps returning: Kafka, built as a log, made queue-style consumption production-ready in 2026.

choices.choice: Store and forward instead of direct calls
choices.why: The queue holds the message, so sender and receiver don’t need to be up, or equally fast, at the same time. Bursts pile up in the queue instead of overwhelming the receiver.

choices.choice: Each message goes to one consumer
choices.why: Competing workers share the load, so throughput grows by adding workers, and each job is done once rather than by everyone.
A message is removed only when a consumer confirms it, so a crash mid-job means redelivery rather than loss. The trade-off is that a consumer can see a message twice and must be idempotent.
Queues were built to move work, not store it, which keeps them simple. Replaying old messages needs a stream instead.
